body.text: On the fiftieth anniversary last year of the Whitlam government’s dismissal, neither of the main characters had much evolved in the popular consciousness. Gough Whitlam was revered, at least on the left, as a progressive warrior and constitutional martyr. In a major speech marking the anniversary, prime minister Anthony Albanese paid tribute to the “stature and significance” of Whitlam’s government.

Sir John Kerr, the governor-general who infamously dismissed the elected Labor government to resolve the parliamentary deadlock and precipitate an election, remained the obvious villain of the affair.

But less was said about opposition leader Malcolm Fraser’s outsized role in the events of October and November 1975. An austere grazier from rural Victoria, Fraser was a formidable but surprisingly aloof politician. His brinksmanship and tactical opportunism precipitated the crisis, and he proved its ultimate beneficiary. As prime minister, he won three elections on the trot and enjoyed the fourth-longest tenure in Australia’s history.

Yet Fraser and his government occupy an awkward place in Australia’s national story. The dismissal is an obvious reason but not the only one, and I’d suggest not even the most important. Albanese mentioned Fraser by name just once in his anniversary oration — and then as a way of complimenting Whitlam — but he was in South Africa a few days later celebrating Fraser’s “principled opposition” to apartheid and racism generally. (The Coalition parties, who in mid-November 2025 were squabbling over leadership and abandoning their net-zero emissions policy, had no time for these anniversaries.)

What should we make of the Fraser government? Was there such a thing as the “Fraser era,” and if so, was anything distinctive about it? And given the commemorative scripts for his contemporaries and successors are so well worn, why do we remain ambivalent about locating Fraser’s government and leadership in Australia’s history?

Partly, it’s a problem of periodisation. History-makers have tended to narrate Australia in the Fraser years as wholly derivative of what came before or after it. Press gallery journalists, in their daily scribblings and larger published narratives, have tended to describe Fraser’s government as the “unexciting break” between more interesting and consequential Labor governments, as the journalist Paul Kelly observed. Historians have rarely disagreed.

Partisan mythmakers have done their bit to cement that impression. Former Labor deputy leader Jenny Macklin, who experienced the Fraser years as a young feminist and parliamentary researcher, recently described the period as the “political interregnum that separated the cultural starburst of Whitlam from the economic renewal of the Hawke–Keating era.” It’s an insight laced with anachronism and nostalgia, but it beautifully captures a dominant way of summing up that era.

It’s also about projection. Politicians have used the Fraser years as a canvas for painting their own pictures of modern Australia. Even when the going got tough for Fraser’s successors in government, Bob Hawke and Paul Keating found mileage in the argument that the “modern industrial Australia” they were making was a vast improvement on the one they inherited from Fraser and the Coalition.

As the Liberal Party sketched out its own reform agenda for the 1980s, they too found it useful to reimagine the Fraser years as “lost” or “wasted.” Periodic disputes erupted between Fraser and his former treasurer John Howard, who brought to his own leadership of the opposition (1985–89) a cultivated identity as a keen reformer frustrated in government by a tepid, immovable prime minister.

More recently the receding memory of the Fraser era offered a stage for competing performances of liberalism and progressivism. Progressives and Labor partisans elevated Fraser as a model of “colour blindness” (to quote The Hawke Memoirs) and a champion of mainstream multiculturalism. Conservatives and right-wingers projected an image of failure onto Fraser-era policies — the pursuit of woolly-headed multiculturalism, the acceptance of refugees from Indochina, the “concession” to Lebanese refugees fleeing civil war. Immigration minister Peter Dutton provoked ire in 2016 with his claim that the latter decision had been “a mistake.” Such politicking had to do less with the actual past than with the opportunity for rhetorical combat in the present.

Today, with conservatives largely in control of the modern Liberal Party, Fraser’s creed of liberalism is anathema. In an interview for Sydney’s Daily Telegraph late last year, Angus Taylor ranked Fraser (along with Malcolm Turnbull) at the “back of the pack” of modern Liberal prime ministers. Fraser’s chief redeeming quality, Taylor seemed to imply, was that he had been canny enough to beat Whitlam.

The growing tendency to project a soft liberalism or centrism on to Fraser has had other effects in recent years. Fraser was reportedly in conversations about forming a new moderate progressive party before he died in 2015. Many of the same agitators, supporters and donors are now active in the “Voices of” and community independent movements. Fraser-era Liberals such as Ian Macphee and Fred Chaney, with their support for independent candidates, have added weight to the perception of Fraser’s liberalism as part of the teal inheritance.

A third reason for the awkward place of the Fraser era in our national politics is the natural act of forgetting. Nobody aged under sixty ever cast a vote for or against the Fraser government themselves. For the most part, the government was undemonstrative, secretive and eager to avoid the public spectacles of the Whitlam years. Fraser’s most recognisable fragment of oratory — “Life wasn’t meant to be easy,” an allusion to George Bernard Shaw made in a speech a few years before he became Liberal leader — signalled the trudging and unexciting emotional register that would characterise his prime ministership.

With television in the ascendant, definitive images bookended the Fraser government. There was footage of Fraser being jeered on the steps of Parliament on 11 November 1975, and of his ministry’s subsequent swearing in. For Labor partisans, there was satisfying footage of Fraser’s cracked voice and quivering lip on the night of his defeat in March 1983.

But between those milestones, few images of Fraser burned themselves into national consciousness. One potential exception was the prime minister’s cameo role introducing an instalment of Countdown; media scholar Liz Giuffre has pointed out that he was probably “the only man in a ‘straight’ suit ever to appear on the program.”

With all the periodising, projecting and forgetting, I thought there was need of a clearer-eyed appraisal of the Fraser era and its place in the broader sweep of Australia’s political history. The contributors to a special, largely open-access issue of Australian Journal of Politics and History have pared back the various mythologies and political silences to drive forward new debates about the Fraser government and the rapidly changing Australia in which it operated.

For one thing, these were years of rapid economic and industrial change. Women’s employment grew significantly but deindustrialisation was encroaching on the horizon; the era of post-war “full employment” was over, whether people realised or not. Historian Owen Bennett argues that pragmatic trade union leaders were deeply implicated in the weakening of Australia’s political investment in full employment.

The pressing challenge for policymakers was stagflation — the painful combination of high inflation, high unemployment and low economic growth. They looked for new economic frameworks, like Milton Friedman’s monetarism, to address that economic cocktail. Yet, as political economist Michael Beggs convincingly argues, Australia’s experiment with a monetary targeting regime was quickly repurposed as a weapon in a much older struggle over arbitration, wage fixing and income distribution.

The Fraser years coincided with the waxing and waning of a cold war détente. Fraser’s government courted China, distrusted the Soviet Union and consistently stressed the importance of the US alliance, which needed careful analysis when Americans elected a new president in 1976. Democrat Jimmy Carter brought to the White House an interest in “trilateralism,” which privileged American, European and Japanese leadership in global affairs. Athanasios Antonopoulos shows that the weight of Fraser’s character and office mattered in conveying Australia’s concerns about its role and influence in such a vision of the world.

Fraser himself had a keen interest in North–South issues and fairness within the British Commonwealth of Nations, but this was not an era free of security concern. James Mortensen and Sue Thompson show that terrorism (of the domestic and transnational varieties) loomed as a growing threat. In 1978, that threat was realised at the Hilton Hotel in Sydney, which was bombed during a Commonwealth Heads of Government regional meeting there.

The federal government acted swiftly, sending troops to protect the visiting dignitaries during their retreat to the Southern Highlands town of Bowral in the days that followed. That deployment raised serious legal and logistical questions that, according to Mortensen and Thompson, could well have been anticipated and better handled.

The Fraser government was also a rhetorical champion of non-discriminatory immigration. Following a lull, migration increased under Fraser. Responding to a major review of post-arrival services for migrants, the government invested in better English language education programs, translation services in health and a Special Broadcasting Service for ethnic audiences.

Yet race and migration continued to be problematic in Australian public discourse. George Bishi and Ana Stevenson show how the media debate over white migrants (some called them refugees) from Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe) reflected a great deal of anxiety about Australia’s humanitarian immigration program. Conservatives in the Liberal Party were sympathetic to fellow adherents of British race patriotism; activists and student groups were critical of the government’s rhetorical fluidity on the issue.

It could be difficult, too, to square the government’s multicultural benevolence with its economic austerity. Rachel Stevens, Mary Tomsic and Jen Rose describe how the North Richmond Family Care Centre in Melbourne, which catered for migrant communities, endured a declining stream of public funding. They describe the ideological inconsistency inherent in that situation as the Fraser paradox.

Not only were there more people in Australia; there were new and competing expectations of government. Conservationists persuaded government to ban sand mining on Fraser Island and oil drilling in the Great Barrier Reef. Alessandro Antonello argues that the Fraser years were distinguished in the broader sweep of Australia’s history by new approaches to oceanic governance and marine policy, replete with a ban on whaling. But a fresh cohort of green activists felt Fraser distinguished himself in a different way, by refusing to defend the Franklin River in Tasmania from damming.

A new type of politics was cultivated in the Northern Territory, which was given self-government in the late 1970s. A new Northern Territory Land Rights Act, developed under Whitlam, facilitated the return of land to traditional owners. That initiative crystallised the competing expectations at play in northern Australia. Jessica Urwin revisits the mining industry campaigns in favour of development and against NT land rights, foreshadowing the bitter — and more familiar — debates that followed in the Hawke and Keating years.

Clearly, the Fraser era was not smooth sailing for reformers. The feminist activists who secured unprecedented access to political power under Whitlam came up against an ethos of restraint and austerity in Canberra from 1975 onward. Debates about Commonwealth support for women’s refuges and funding for the new Family Law Court showed that plenty of people around the cabinet table believed in the austerity imperative.

Those involved in the action, though, could see the continuities with the Whitlam government, and not only in hindsight. Sara Dowse, a towering figure in the history of Australia’s feminist public service practitioners — or “femocrats” as they are often called — reflects in this special issue on the consistency she observed between the Whitlam and Fraser years from her vantage point at the Office of Women’s Affairs.

In the years after it lost government in 1983 the Fraser government was increasingly viewed as having tried little and achieved less. The economic outcomes spoke for themselves — at the time of the government’s defeat, unemployment (seasonally adjusted) stood at 10 per cent of the workforce, consumer price inflation ran at 11.4 per cent and a new recession had left Australia with negative 2 per cent GDP growth for the year to March 1983.

It became received wisdom that the government was inhibited from the outset by the divisive manner of its arrival. The prime minister’s caution, this line of thinking runs, was a result of his “legitimacy problem.” But the contributors to the special issue showed the world did not simply sit still and wait for a more exciting leader and era to arrive.

There was always more to the government than the manner of its coming and then the satisfaction — for Labor partisans especially — of its going. More than seven years and three election victories came in between. There were major shifts in political thought and discourse that seemed “radical and new” to a generation of policymakers reared on Australia’s social liberalism. There was a steady succession of public inquiries and royal commissions on matters great and small. Cataloguing those inquiries for this collection, Scott Prasser identifies something of a continuity with the Whitlam experiment in government.

Fraser himself was quite late to join in the struggle over his legacy. Occasional biographies included one by political scientist Patrick Weller, published in 1989. Weller reflects on the making of that biography and the unparalleled access to official documents as well as insider testimonies. In 2010, Fraser and his co-author Margaret Simons released a comprehensive account of the former prime minister’s life and times, but this came nearly three decades after his political dénouement.

Zeroing in on the Fraser years allows us to reconsider aspects of political change in late twentieth-century Australia that have been inadequately excavated to date. The contributions to this special issue help interrogate simplistic periodisations of recent Australian politics, and pare back layers of political projection so that readers can see an important chapter of the nation’s past with fresh eyes. •
